 Jeremy Fears Jr. (1) and Jasiah Jervis (25) combined for 28 points in Tuesday's win over Duke. Nam Y. Huh / AP Photo 
 By Brendan Marks Nov. 11, 2026 Updated Share article 59 CHICAGO — Jeremy Fears Jr. had just started making his way to the showers inside Michigan State’s locker room when, at 9:09 p.m. local time, the FaceTime call came in.
 And when Earvin ‘Magic’ Johnson calls, you answer.
 Fears did, of course, immediately throw the call on speakerphone as he meandered to a convenient (and quiet) corner of Michigan State’s locker room inside the United Center.
 Advertisement
 There — barefoot, leaning against a trash can, with Tom Izzo proudly eavesdropping from the nearby coaches locker room — the best point guard in college basketball could only smirk and smile as the best Spartan of all time congratulated him on the best win of this young college basketball season: No. 5 Michigan State’s 79-73 victory over No. 2 Duke in Tuesday night’s Champions Classic opener.
 But as Johnson heaped congratulations on Fears — whose master class performance included a game-high 18 points and 11 assists, plus seven rebounds, a block and a steal — Izzo, listening from a room over, couldn’t help himself.
 What about Fears’ five missed free throws? Or his four turnovers? 
 “Tell ‘em what you would’ve done, Earvin!” Izzo joked as he exited the locker room, peering over Fears’ phone as he did.
 All three program icons — one past, one present and one who connects the two — laughed, before Fears and Johnson hung up a second later.
 Tyran Stokes shines, Michigan State stifles Duke's offense Brendan Marks But what Izzo said lingered, even if not in a way he meant.
 What Johnson would’ve done? Well … in many ways, it was what Fears just did:
 Lead the Spartans to a statement win — MSU’s first over an AP top-two opponent since 2021 — while rubber-stamping them as legitimate national championship contenders.
 “We haven’t taken a back seat to anybody,” Izzo said, “and I don’t plan on taking a back seat in the near future or in the far future, to be honest with you.”
 Sure, that’s easy to say after one of the program’s best regular-season wins in years. But frankly, that mentality from Izzo in the first place is also why Michigan State was able to do what it did Tuesday: by sticking with the longtime tenets of a two-time championship program.
 Even in this transformational era of college athletics, where the transfer portal and eligibility chaos and payments to players seemingly reign supreme, Izzo has endured undeterred, leaning into retention and development and the type of “tough love” coaching that is less widespread than ever. He’s not the only one to do so — look at fellow title contenders Florida, Virginia and UConn for further evidence — but that strategy is clearly the exception to the rule at this point in the arc of college athletics.
 Advertisement
 Has that philosophy cost him certain talent at times in recent seasons? Of course. You think Izzo wanted such anemic offenses of late, when it at times felt like Michigan State was trying to milk a stone? Not at all.
 But to stick to his principles, that’s the compromise.
 Instead, he bet on guys like Fears and Coen Carr — and to a lesser extent, Jordan Scott and Cam Ward — and kept sanding the edges, month after month, year after year, until it looked the way he wanted.
 Until it looked like a group that could join the 1979 and 2000 teams in the Breslin Center rafters.
 And Tuesday, in emphatic fashion, Sparty proved it absolutely has what it takes to make the short drive this April from East Lansing to Detroit, the site of this season’s Final Four.
 Jordan Scott was a human fence against Drew Scharnowski and Duke, recording a staggering five first-half blocks. (Michael Reaves / Getty Images) “Just a stepping stone,” Fears called Tuesday’s win, in the understatement of the century.
 From the opening whistle, Michigan State was clearly playing a different game than the Blue Devils, who — despite their roster of future NBAers — never matched Sparty’s physicality or want-to. The biggest tone-setter in that respect was Scott, the 6-foot-8 sophomore on the cusp of a breakout. Even against Duke’s formidable frontline, Scott never blinked, turning into a human fence around the rim, recording a staggering five first-half blocks while otherwise disincentivizing the Blue Devils’ drives.
 “About as good a game as you could have for a guy that went 2-for-7, 1-for-4 from the 3,” Izzo joked of Scott. “He probably changed the whole game himself with his defense, with his rebounding, with his effort-related stats.”
 Cut to Duke coach Jon Scheyer, who said MSU “outcompeted us,” and that the vast discrepancy between the two top-five teams was like an “out-of-body experience.”
 And considering Duke shot just 33.3 percent overall and 21.4 percent from 3, he’s not wrong.
 Advertisement
 But what should elate Michigan State fans — and terrify the rest of the Big Ten, if not the nation at large — is how the team won in the second half: with offense . Fears, of course, was a huge part of that, regularly splitting Duke’s hedges on ball screens and getting deep into the paint. From there, it was either an easy layup for himself, or a dump-off to his bigs if the Blue Devils collapsed.
 It wasn’t all Fears, though, even for as good as he was. Take freshman guard Jasiah Jervis, for instance, whose stepback 3 with 5:17 to play stymied Duke’s comeback attempt and pushed the lead back to double figures. Or Scott, whose layup with 1:50 to play gave Sparty juuuust enough breathing room after Duke cut it to a two-possession game. Or Ward, whose pace slowed in the second half, but whose all-out relentlessness attacking the rim still shocked the Blue Devils’ system and led to a 14-point night.
 That’s a lot of firepower for a program which hasn’t had nearly that much in recent seasons.

 But perhaps most impressively of all? That Michigan State never needed a gargantuan comeback or run to put away a team many already had earmarked for the Final Four.
 Sparty simply did what it does at its historic best, and what it hasn’t always been able to the last few seasons:
 It put Duke in the mortar and ground the Blue Devils to death from every direction imaginable.
 “What we’ve been talking about for 20 years,” Izzo said. “Defend, rebound and run.”
 Now, three games into this season is admittedly a bit early to book hotel rooms in the Motor City. The Spartans still have Tennessee, Arkansas and Gonzaga left in the nonconference, too, three more ranked foes who will test Sparty’s winning formula. Then there’s the woodchipper that is the Big Ten, even if this specific team looks like a hand-in-glove fit for the physicality it takes to win in that league.
 Advertisement
 But Tuesday was, perhaps more than at any point since the COVID-19 pandemic, a glimpse of a team that could do something special.
 One that has the talent, the experience and the togetherness to make Michigan State’s final First Four since 2019.
 “We just wanted to play our best brand of basketball,” Fears said, “and hopefully that led to something good.”
